reasons: The quoted passage is primarily a description of what the speaker's organization does, not a clear universal instruction to the audience.
The adjacent source text qualifies this level of activity with a high volume of people coming through tests; the candidate omits that qualifier.
The action and completion condition accurately reflect the source's recommendation to learn from wins, investigate losses, and implement resulting changes in winning and future tests.
The candidate preserves the stated high-volume qualifier and the named cross-functional roles.
The source does not define high volume, and the candidate appropriately records that uncertainty.
This principle directly reflects the source's distinction that quantitative data addresses what is happening and qualitative data addresses why.

The source recommends funnel and drop-off analysis generally, including for stores under 300,000 sessions; it does not limit the recommendation to either under-300,000 stores or ad-to-PDP traffic paths.
The ad-to-PDP condition determines which funnel stages the source specifically names, rather than serving as an alternative trigger for doing funnel analysis.

The source says everyone should use heat maps, using 10,000 and 10 million sessions as examples. The candidate narrows this into a 10,000-to-10-million traffic range, which is not stated as a boundary.
The remaining installation and analysis steps are supported.
The source supports investigating and eliminating false/rage clicks, but it does not establish that this action has a mandatory dependency on the separate heat-map candidate.
The candidate's depends_on relation turns contextual discussion of heat-map analysis into an explicit prerequisite not stated in the excerpt.
The source lists price and offer testing and explicitly frames finding a profitable offer for cold paid media as the way to scale paid media effectively.
The candidate does not invent a method or profitability threshold.
The action accurately combines the source's recommendations for user testing, usability studies, user interviews, and calling customers with the example interview questions.
The two required questions and the instruction to establish post-purchase surveys are supported.

However, the candidate makes the action applicable only when no survey exists, whereas the source treats post-purchase surveys as a non-negotiable and instructs the audience to ensure the questions are asked.
The source wording for the recommended tool is transcription-ambiguous; representing it as two alternatives, 'No Commerce or Komerse,' is not established by the excerpt.
The source expressly says objections from post-purchase responses can be used to change front-end copy or angle and provides the stated results-timing example.
The candidate preserves that example as an example rather than presenting the six-week claim as universally applicable.

The source explicitly gives this alternative for organizations without an existing post-purchase survey but with a customer list to survey, including emailing VIPs/customers and offering a chance to win a $250 Amazon gift card.
The review-mining process and the categories to find are supported.

The source gives a hedged, imprecise volume expression—'over, you know, 500, a thousand reviews'—rather than establishing a 500-to-1,000 numerical trigger. The candidate should retain that uncertainty without converting it into a threshold.

The source recommends testing the store across mobile, desktop, and tablet, observing another person use it, finding obstructive bugs, and conducting full UX/UI audits to ensure a good buying experience.
The central action of combining qualitative and quantitative data and using it for CRO is supported.

Its depends_on relations improperly make particular tactics mandatory prerequisites, including review mining and the specified post-purchase survey candidate. The source instead calls for the two data types in full and includes conditional or alternative collection tactics, such as the one-time survey when no post-purchase survey exists.
The source supports focusing on bolded items under 300,000 sessions and doing all listed qualitative items over the stated threshold.

The candidate expands 'all of this' into a definite requirement to perform all qualitative and quantitative analysis, although the quoted statement occurs in the qualitative-data discussion and does not itself clearly specify both sets.
The excerpt does not provide a time period for the session threshold.
This accurately reports the speaker's assertion that data is the most important item in a CRO arsenal.
The warning itself is supported by the source.

The candidate incorrectly makes the source's single approximately-6% footer-placement example a trigger or prerequisite for the general warning. Important content can be below the fold without that exact example or percentage applying.
The source explicitly lists 'price and offer testing' among the quantitative-analysis must-dos, and the candidate does not add unsupported procedural detail.
The source supports the warning that exit pops and cookie modals/bars can obstruct CTAs or buttons.

The candidate's trigger incorrectly treats one described cookie-bar problem as a condition for the warning about exit pops and cookie modals; these are examples of separate possible bugs, not prerequisites for one another.
Both tool observations are stated in the source: Clarity is described as free and laggy, and heatmap.com is described as tracking revenue rather than only clicks.
However, the candidate's trigger makes the heatmap.com capability conditional on the statement about Clarity. The excerpt states them independently.
The source explicitly characterizes post-purchase surveys as, in the speaker's view, probably the single most effective store-optimization method.
This principle exactly reflects the source's statement that customer surveys and feedback loops are essential.
The source says that under the stated 300,000-session level, organizations need either an agency like the speaker's or the time and resources to do the work themselves.
The source supports the two-to-three-week duration and approximately 100-page audit deliverable for organizations working with the speaker's agency at the higher tier and over 300,000 sessions.
The candidate's prerequisites include only the session volume and omit the stated dependency that the organization is working with that agency/on that higher service tier.
The source does recommend installing Clarity by Microsoft and notes that it is free but laggy.
The alternative_to relation with heatmap.com is unsupported: the source discusses both tools but does not state that they are mutually exclusive alternatives.
The source supports considering heatmap.com and describes it as revenue-based rather than click-only.
The alternative_to relation with Clarity is not stated. The excerpt presents both tools without requiring a choice between them.
This is clearly framed as the source's example, preserving its approximate 6% figure and placement just above the footer rather than asserting it as a universal result.
The source says the first stated survey question can reveal purchase motivations and gives wanting to lose weight as an example.
The source says many people may complete surveys when they are sent, in a passage following a suggested prize draw.
It does not establish that incentives increase completion, nor does it provide a comparison or causal evidence. The candidate's title makes that unsupported causal claim.

source_limitations: The excerpt begins mid-sentence and ends mid-sentence, so surrounding conditions and the remainder of the final audit description are unavailable.
This is a spoken, apparently auto-transcribed workshop excerpt. Several terms are ambiguous or malformed, including 'G4,' 'three thou 100,000,' 'no commerce, Komerse,' 'heruristic,' and 'modles.'

The source refers to bolded non-negotiables on slides, but the formatting and complete slide contents are not included, so the full under- versus over-300,000-session requirements cannot be reconstructed.
The 300,000-session threshold is not tied to a stated measurement period in the excerpt.

Several performance statements are speaker assertions or anecdotes, including claims about revenue uplift, survey responses, profitability, and the approximately 6% scroll-depth example; the excerpt supplies no underlying methodology or evidence.
